node.label: Anna Lowenhaupt Tsing
node.date_label: Friction (2005) · “Unruly Edges” (2012) · The Mushroom at the End of the World (2015) · Feral Atlas, co-edited (2020)
node.description: An anthropologist who studies how global capitalism and environmental change are made in particular places. In Friction: An Ethnography of Global Connection (2005), set in the rainforests of Indonesia, she proposed friction instead of a “clash” of cultures as the figure for how global connections work: conflicting, awkward and sometimes productive. The Mushroom at the End of the World (2015) follows the matsutake mushroom through disturbed forests and commodity chains to ask what collaborative life remains possible in capitalist ruins. In “Sorting Out Commodities” (2013) she extends Marx’s primitive accumulation, arguing that capitalism keeps depending on non-capitalist relations. A 2015 essay calls a related process “salvage accumulation”: the conversion of goods and skills made outside capitalism into capitalist value. In “Sorting Out Commodities” (2013), she criticises accounts that treat capitalism as a coherent whole, naming Hardt and Negri’s Empire (2000) in the main text and David Harvey in note 24. “Unruly Edges” (2012), dedicated to Donna Haraway, extends Haraway’s companion species to fungi, draws on Sidney Mintz’s histories of sugar for its account of plantations, and proposes multispecies landscapes as protagonists of world history. She co-edited Arts of Living on a Damaged Planet: Ghosts and Monsters of the Anthropocene (2017) with Nils Bubandt, Elaine Gan and Heather Anne Swanson, and Feral Atlas: The More-than-Human Anthropocene (2020) with Jennifer Deger, Alder Keleman Saxena and Feifei Zhou. The Society for Cultural Anthropology gave The Mushroom at the End of the World its 2016 Bateson Prize. In the society’s 2017 forum on the book, Katherine Sacco asked how its idea of the “latent commons” works in cities. Replying, Tsing conceded that the latent commons “is hardly a robust political program”. A 2021 talk abstract asks whether history was “denied” in an early essay by Dipesh Chakrabarty and how historians might approach the Anthropocene.
node.representative_figures_and_works: In the Realm of the Diamond Queen (1993); Friction: An Ethnography of Global Connection (2005); Words in Motion: Toward a Global Lexicon (2009, co-edited with Carol Gluck); “Unruly Edges: Mushrooms as Companion Species” (2012); “Sorting Out Commodities” (2013); The Mushroom at the End of the World: On the Possibility of Life in Capitalist Ruins (2015); Arts of Living on a Damaged Planet (2017, co-edited); Feral Atlas: The More-than-Human Anthropocene (2020, co-edited).
node.scope_note: “Unruly Edges” (2012), “Sorting Out Commodities” (2013) and “Salvage Accumulation” (2015) were read in full on open journal routes. Tsing’s 2017 forum response and the 2019 Edge Effects conversation highlights were also read. Friction and The Mushroom at the End of the World are unread: Friction is described from its publisher’s text and The Mushroom at the End of the World from the Society for Cultural Anthropology’s prize citation and forum. Only the abstract of the 2021 talk was read; the talk and the Chakrabarty essay it leaves unnamed remain unread. Arts of Living on a Damaged Planet and Feral Atlas are listed by title; their dates come from the bibliographic record, and neither was read for argument.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Unruly Edges: Mushrooms as Companion Species” (2012), an essay dedicated to Haraway, Tsing says she is indebted to Haraway for the concept of companion species and for permission to refuse the boundary between nature and culture.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 141 (dedication “for Donna Haraway”; abstract: “Haraway’s concept of companion species takes us beyond familiar companions”; second paragraph: “This essay is indebted to Donna Haraway not only for the concept of ‘companion species’”) with n. 1 citing The Companion Species Manifesto (2003); p. 145 n. 12 (“Haraway’s work on dogs is a key interruption”); acknowledgements p. 153 (Haraway gave “a most generous critical reading”). A stated debt in Tsing’s own text. Haraway’s Manifesto not reread here.
proposed_edges.map_label: Mutual exchange: companion species, refugia and the Plantationocene

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Unruly Edges” (2012), Tsing’s account of plantation sugar draws on Mintz: she quotes Puerto Rican cane workers from Worker in the Cane (1974) and cites Sweetness and Power (1985) for sugar’s late arrival as an object of mass consumption and for the plantation as a proto-industrial labour model.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 148–149: body text on sugar cane, coerced plantation labour and rum before mass consumption (“Long before sugar became an object and symbol of mass consumption”). Note 27 quotes Puerto Rican cane workers from Worker in the Cane, p. 16; note 30: “Caribbean sugar plantations formed a proto-industrial labor model that shaped nascent industrialisation in Europe”. Body text engages Mintz’s argument; it is not a passing citation. Mintz’s books not read here.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Unruly Edges” (2012), Tsing’s passage on white women as agents of racial hygiene in plantation colonies cites Stoler’s Carnal Knowledge and Imperial Power (2002) for the argument that the transformation of gender was key to emerging ideologies of race and medicine, and for the importance of white women’s migration to the tropics to late-colonial eugenics.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 149 (“White women became agents of racial hygiene”) through p. 150; n. 31: “Ann Stoler shows how the transformation of gender was key to emergent ideologies of race and medicine”; n. 32: Stoler “shows the centrality of the importation of white women to the tropics to the new eugenics”. The body argument is built on the cited work. Stoler’s book not read here.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Unruly Edges” (2012), Tsing follows Latour’s The Pasteurization of France (French original 1984; she cites the Sheridan and Law translation) in treating colonial spaces in the tropics as the first living laboratories of Pasteurian hygiene.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 150 body: “Pasteurian germ theory was tested and boosted in the tropics, where white-controlled spaces could be organised as laboratories”; n. 32: “As Bruno Latour explains … Latour suggests that colonial armies in the tropics … were the first living laboratories for Pasteurian medicine”. Tsing’s note and bibliography cite the Harvard translation by Sheridan and Law, dated 1986 in her bibliography (the publisher’s date is not checked here); the French original is 1984. A bounded borrowing; Latour’s book not read here.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Sorting Out Commodities” (2013), Tsing extends Marx’s primitive accumulation, arguing that capitalism never transcends it but keeps depending on it, and she follows Marx in defining the capitalist commodity by alienation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 21: “Marx’s term ‘primitive accumulation’ is useful in extension: Capitalism does not transcend primitive accumulation, but continues to depend on it.” P. 22 n. 1: “I define commodities by the alienation that constitutes them. In doing so, I follow Marx ([1867] 1992)”. P. 24: factory discipline “created what Marx ([1844] 1959) called ‘alienation’”. An extension, not an orthodox application. Her 2015 essay names a related process “salvage accumulation” without citing Marx.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Sorting Out Commodities” (2013), Tsing sets her capitalism-specific definition of the commodity against Appadurai’s, which treats any good in exchange as a commodity and, she argues, sidesteps the specificity of capitalism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read p. 22 n. 1: “Appadurai (2012), for example, defines commodities as any goods in exchange. This allows him to sidestep the specificity of capitalism … Following Kopytoff (1986), Appadurai rejects a gift-commodity distinction”. The note frames the article’s central gift–commodity contrast (body, pp. 21–22). Tsing cites Appadurai’s 2012 essay “Commodities and the politics of value”, not The Social Life of Things (1986). A definitional contrast, not a general critique; Appadurai’s essay unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Sorting Out Commodities” (2013), Tsing criticises accounts that picture capitalism as a singular, enclosed and coherent system; a note places Harvey’s The Limits to Capital (1982; cited in the 2007 edition) beside Hardt and Negri’s Empire as such an account, and she argues that these analyses miss the open-ended, contingent processes through which capitalism is made.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read pp. 38–39: “it has become increasingly popular for critics to imagine capitalism as a singular, enclosed, and coherent system”; n. 24: “Similarly, David Harvey (2007) shows capitalism as a coherent whole; like Hardt and Negri (2000), he aims to inspire resistance against this whole”; p. 39: “such analyses miss the open-ended processes”. Tsing cites the 2007 Verso edition of a 1982 book. A short critique within the conclusion; Harvey’s book unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Against capitalism as a closed whole

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Unruly Edges” (2012), Tsing proposes multispecies landscapes as protagonists of world history, and in 2021 she asked historians to treat nonhumans as fully historical actors in histories of the Anthropocene.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Unruly Edges, p. 141 abstract: “This essay opens a door to multispecies landscapes as protagonists for histories of the world”; the essay follows fungi through “the last ten thousand years of human disturbance history”. OSU abstract (2021), question (3): “What happens when we recognize nonhumans as fully historical — and thus mutable actors in the making of more-than-human histories?” Programmatic statements by Tsing; uptake by environmental historians is not claimed. Edge Effects (2019) adds her stated reason for keeping the term Anthropocene: it “allows interdisciplinary conversation between natural scientists and humanists”.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Sorting Out Commodities” (2013), Tsing argues that describing the rough edges of capitalist supply chains is a job for ethnographers, and that multispecies ethnography meets political economy in an emerging field; the 2016 Bateson Prize citation calls her Mushroom book storytelling-as-ethnography.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: HAU 2013, p. 39: “Describing those rough edges is a job for ethnographers”; “Multispecies ethnography meets political economy in this emerging field.” SCA announcement (2016), jury paragraph: “an open-ended polyphonic assemblage that performs in writing the very concepts it generates”; “Through such storytelling-as-ethnography she traces …”. The prize citation is the society’s reading, not Tsing’s own claim; the book is unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Friction (2005), as its publisher describes it, replaces the view that globalization means a clash of cultures with friction as a figure for the conflicting interactions of global connection, and offers methods for studying global interconnections.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: AES 2005 Senior Book Prize page, reproduced publisher’s description: “Challenging the widespread view that globalization invariably signifies a ‘clash’ of cultures, anthropologist Anna Tsing here develops friction in its place as a metaphor”; “Providing a portfolio of methods to study global interconnections … and how much is overlooked in contemporary theories of the global.” Publisher description only; the book is unread. AES dates it 2004; Tsing cites it as 2005 (Unruly Edges, n. 39).

proposed_edges.relationship: In Planetary Longings (2022), Mary Louise Pratt draws on Anna Lowenhaupt Tsing’s Friction (2005) to interpret encounters with global capitalism as generative, unpredictable world-making.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s licensed introduction, especially pp. 5–9. Pratt explains Tsing’s concept in the body of her own argument. The preview’s p. 8 gives 2004, but p. 9 cites 2005; the original publication year is 2005. No claim about chapters outside the preview.
proposed_edges.map_label: Friction and world-making in Planetary Longings

proposed_edges.relationship: According to Sarah Bellows-Blakely’s “Empowering African Girls?” (2023), Antoinette Burton’s Africa in the Indian Imagination (2016) draws on Tsing’s Friction (2005) to analyze the uneasy, productive tensions underpinning transnational alliances.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher-served article PDF, specifically this paragraph and note 12. The preceding clause explicitly attributes Burton’s framework to Tsing and another scholar; the note identifies both books. Burton’s original passage remains unread. This is a qualified, mediated application under the relationship protocol.

proposed_edges.relationship: Tsing’s “Inside the Economy of Appearances” (2000) and Friction (2005) contribute an account of capitalist investment through performance and imagined economic futures, substantively discussed by Christensen and Ivarsson in “Global Capitalist Assemblages” (first published 2025).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s open text around notes 48–52 and its references. This is a named conceptual contribution to historical analysis of capitalism, not a shared-topic inference. The original Tsing works were not newly read for this edge.
proposed_edges.map_label: Performance and imagined futures in capitalist investment
